# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles site-level demographic series for 1.216 excavated and surveyed prehistoric settlements across 24 modern territories in North Africa, the Near East, Anatolia, Cyprus, Transcaucasia, Iran and Afghanistan from 10000BC to 3200BC. Grouped into six macro-regional tables—the Levant and Cyprus (321 sites), Anatolia and Transcaucasia (246 sites), the Nile Valley and Delta (317 sites), Mesopotamia and the Arabian Peninsula (182 sites), Iran and Afghanistan (134 sites) and the Maghreb and Atlantic Sahara (16 sites)—the entries document the transition from mobile Epipalaeolithic camps to PPNB megasites and terminal Chalcolithic proto-urban towns. Across the inventory, peak populations cluster in the 2k to 6,5k bracket at long-lived farming tells such as Çatalhöyük, Çayönü, Jericho, Tell Abu Hureyra, 'Ain Ghazal, Susa and Merimde, before southern Mesopotamian canal centres at Ur, Uruk and Kish pull away to 17,6k inhabitants by 3200BC [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Palmisano2019Holocene]. Site coordinates and occupancy spans are cross-referenced against regional excavation monographs, radiocarbon inventories and geoBoundaries subadministrative meshes [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].



# Background

Excavated settlement mounds (*tells*, *höyüks* and *tepes*), open-air riverine camps and desert *escargotières* provide the primary building blocks for prehistoric population history across Western Asia and North Africa. Whereas later chapters rely on tax registers, hearth counts and provincial censuses, the seven millennia from 10000BC to 3200BC must be pieced together from stratigraphic exposures, architectural floor plans and radiocarbon-dated occupation horizons [@Moore1978Neolithic; @Finlayson2011Architectu; @Palmisano2019Holocene].

Throughout this span, settlement forms evolved alongside subsistence strategies. Late Natufian and PPNA hamlets in the Levant—such as Nahal Ein Gev II, Wadi Faynan 16, Shubayqa 6 and Saaïdé II—consisted of clustered semi-subterranean round huts built from undressed fieldstone and mud plaster [@Grosman2016Nahal; @Horvath2001Natufian; @Thuesen2023Nascent]. By the Middle and Late PPNB, rectilinear mudbrick houses and multi-storeyed stone compounds allowed populations of several thousand people to pack onto single hillside springs at 'Ain Ghazal, Ba'ja, Beidha, Yiftahel and Tell Qarassa [@Balbo2012Squaring; @BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Benz2019Burying; @SapirHen2016Human]. Similar high-density aggregations appeared on the Konya Plain at Çatalhöyük [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Wright2013Domesticat], along the Ergani plain at Çayönü, on the Susiana plain at Susa and Chogha Mish, and eventually along the lower Euphrates and Nile floodplains.

# Methodology

Each entry in this gazetteer derives from published excavation reports, national archaeological site registers and regional survey monographs. Occupied spans are tabulated at 500-year intervals from 10000BC through 3500BC, closing at the 3200BC terminal Chalcolithic benchmark. For clarity of comparison across six columns, the regional tables display geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude in decimal degrees with European comma separators) together with population estimates at three anchor horizons: the Epipalaeolithic opening at 10000BC, the mature Ceramic Neolithic at 6000BC and the terminal Chalcolithic at 3200BC. Hyphens denote horizons before site foundation or after abandonment.

Where residential architecture is well preserved, site populations are estimated from excavated roofed floor area, contemporaneous dwelling ratios and household multipliers ranging from 4,5 persons in circular PPNA huts to 6,5 persons in rectilinear PPNB and Chalcolithic compounds [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Kadowaki2012Household]. Where surface sherd scatter and mound area provide the only volumetric measure, site totals follow standard Near Eastern tell density calibrations adjusted for courtyard and craft-quarter fractions [@Palmisano2019Holocene; @Wright2013Domesticat]. All site points sit inside the metric-isotropic Voronoi catchment mesh described in the companion literature review, anchored to geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] so that site-level estimates remain strictly consistent with the 16 catchment totals.

# Testing and Validation

Every catalogued settlement was audited for coordinate integrity, chronological bounds and rank-size coherence across the 10000BC to 3200BC window. Coordinates were verified against published site gazetteers and modern hydrographic networks to ensure zero offshore stranding outside Cyprus and Bahrain, and zero modern metropolitan back-projection into uninhabited desert basins. Across all 1.216 sites, the rank-size regression yields a Zipf slope of 0,37 ($R^2 = 0,77$), confirming that prehistoric villages remained relatively flat in size hierarchy prior to the emergence of southern Mesopotamian state centres at Ur, Uruk and Kish in the late fourth millennium BC.

In the Levant, catalogued peaks for Beidha, 'Ain Ghazal, Yiftahel, Teleilat Ghassul and Tell Abu Hureyra were checked against independent household and osteological studies [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Slon2014Plastered; @Munro2018Emergence]. In Anatolia, Çatalhöyük East's long 6k to 6,5k plateau accords with archaeobotanical and ground-stone evidence for sustained 1.500-year occupation [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Coulardeau2023Sedentaris]. In northern Arabia and the Negev-Sinai fringe, sites such as Al Uyaynah, Jebel Oraf 108 and Nahal Roded 110 were verified against recent survey dates from the Early Holocene wet phase [@Crassard2013Beyond; @Birkenfeld2020Hunting; @Alasmari2026Results].

# Results

## Levant, Sinai and Cyprus

Table \ref{tab:zone1} lists 321 catalogued settlements across Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Cyprus, spanning Natufian hamlets, PPNB megasites, Pottery Neolithic Yarmukian villages and early Cypriot coastal settlements [@Moore1978Neolithic; @Yerkes2012Form; @Shtienberg2020Neolithic]. Along the Jordan Rift and Damascus basin, early round-house camps at Jericho, WF16, Nahal Ein Gev II and Shubayqa 6 gave way to dense rectilinear compounds at 'Ain Ghazal, Teleilat Ghassul, Sha'ar Hagolan, Yiftahel and Tell Abu Hureyra [@Finlayson2011Architectu; @Grosman2016Nahal; @Thuesen2023Nascent]. Across the sea on Cyprus, Aetokremnos, Klimonas, Kalavasos-Tenta, Choirokoitia and Lemba Lakkous document maritime colonisation from the tenth millennium BC onward.

## Anatolia and Transcaucasia

Table \ref{tab:zone2} presents 246 excavated mounds and hilltop sites across Turkey, Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan, tracing the spread of farming from southeastern Anatolian Pre-Pottery sanctuaries through central Anatolian mudbrick towns to Kura-Aras villages [@Biltekin2024Exploring; @Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Budja2009Early]. Upper Tigris and Euphrates sites such as Çayönü and Göbekli Tepe sit alongside central and western Anatolian mounds including Çatalhöyük, Kuruçay Höyük, Yumuktepe, Ulucak Höyük and Yeşilova Höyük, while Böyük Kesik, Samshvilde and Tsaghkahovit anchor the Kura-Aras piedmont corridor.

## Nile Valley, Delta and Western Oases

Table \ref{tab:zone3} documents 317 predynastic settlements, Fayum shore camps and oasis stations across Egypt, reflecting the gradual convergence of Epipalaeolithic fishers and Saharan cattle herders onto the Nile alluvium prior to 3200BC. Delta mounds such as Tell el-Samara and Merimde Beni Salame link Lower Egypt with Fayum lake basins around Krokodilopolis and Upper Egyptian cultivation centres at Hermopolis Magna, Kaine and Latopolis.

## Mesopotamia and Arabian Peninsula

Table \ref{tab:zone4} records 182 settlements across Iraq, Oman, Yemen, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, linking northern Hassuna-Halaf rain-fed villages and southern Ubaid-Uruk cities with Holocene wet-phase Arabian camps [@Crassard2013Beyond; @Alasmari2026Results]. In northern Iraq, Tell Arpachiyah and Tepe Gawra document early painted-pottery farming networks, while on the lower alluvium Ur, Uruk, Kish, Nippur and Tell Yassir illustrate the fourth-millennium leap to urban scale. Across Arabia, Al-Khasbah in Oman, Hajar Bin Humeid in Yemen and Jebel Oraf 108 in the Nefud highlight wet-phase pastoral and coastal subsistence.

## Iranian Plateau, Zagros and Afghanistan

Table \ref{tab:zone5} compiles 134 settlements across Iran and Afghanistan, extending from Zagros aceramic camps and Susiana tells across the central plateau oases to the Hindu Kush foothills and Badakhshan. Western Iranian sites such as Susa, KS-108 and Hajji Firuz Tepe pair with northern and central plateau tells including Tepe Hissar, Tepe Sagzabad and Yarim Tepe, while T. Fullol, Makonimor, Dekhonaba and Tarinkot represent early proto-urban and pastoral nodes across Afghanistan.

# Limitations

Site-level coverage across this 1.216-settlement gazetteer mirrors regional excavation histories. Dense rescue surveys in Israel, Jordan, western Syria, central Anatolia, Lower Egypt and southwestern Iran supply hundreds of geo-referenced mounds, whereas interior Libya, Yemen, Atlantic Morocco and upland Afghanistan are represented only by key excavated type sites and oasis surveys. Consequently, individual site counts in Table \ref{tab:zone6} or the Afghan subset reflect fieldwork density rather than total rural hamlet numbers, which are instead captured at the regional catchment level through kriged habitat covariates and demographic multipliers.

Furthermore, lateral settlement drift across multi-period tells means that peak figures around 6,5k at major Neolithic mounds represent maximum multi-phase occupational envelopes rather than unbroken single-generation censuses. Alluvial siltation across the lower Euphrates and Nile Delta, together with post-glacial sea-level rise along the eastern Mediterranean and Persian Gulf coasts, also masks submerged or buried Epipalaeolithic camps older than 6000BC [@Shtienberg2020Neolithic; @Roberts2017Human]. Finally, shifting radiocarbon calibration curves across the ninth and seventh millennia BC introduce centennial uncertainty around exact foundation and abandonment dates, meaning individual horizon columns should be interpreted alongside the broader regional trends analysed in the companion review.

# Conclusion

Together, these six regional tables anchor the spatial distribution of prehistoric population from the Atlantic Maghreb to the Hindu Kush. They document the gradual scaling-up of human communities from small Epipalaeolithic bands into permanent agricultural villages by 6000BC, and finally into the first irrigated urban centres of southern Mesopotamia and predynastic Egypt by 3200BC.
